q: According to Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, without review, when do we lose most of what we just learned?
why: Fast at first. Forgetting is steepest early, then levels off. Reviewing at growing intervals — spaced repetition — resets the curve each time and makes memories last.

statement: Multitasking makes you more productive on complex work.
why: False. The brain switches between tasks rather than doing them in parallel, and each switch costs time and accuracy. Some estimates put the loss at up to 40% of productive time.

title: Writing tomorrow's to-do list before bed helped people fall asleep faster.
detail: In a 2018 Baylor University study, participants who spent five minutes writing a to-do list fell asleep about nine minutes faster than those who wrote about tasks they'd already completed.

q: Using the Rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 8% annual return?
why: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. The rule approximates compound growth. At 3% it takes 24 years; at 12%, just 6. It also works in reverse for inflation eating your savings.

statement: Being awake for 17–19 hours impairs performance about as much as a 0.05% blood alcohol level.
why: True. A 2000 study found that after 17–19 hours without sleep, performance on several tests matched or was worse than at 0.05% blood alcohol — the legal driving limit in many countries.

title: Walking boosted people's creative output by about 60% in a Stanford study.
detail: In 2014 experiments, participants came up with more creative uses for everyday objects while walking — even on a treadmill facing a wall — than while sitting.

q: The Dunning–Kruger effect describes how people with low skill in an area tend to…
why: Overestimate. The skills needed to perform well are often the same ones needed to recognize good performance, so beginners can't see their own mistakes.

title: Plan with "when X, I will Y"
body: Vague goals like "exercise more" rarely stick. Linking an action to a specific trigger — "when I finish lunch, I'll walk for ten minutes" — makes it far more likely to happen.
challenge: Write one "when X, I will Y" plan for a habit you've been putting off, and do it today.

statement: Rereading your notes is one of the most effective ways to study.
why: False. Rereading feels productive because the material looks familiar. Testing yourself — retrieval practice — consistently produces much better long-term memory.

q: In a negotiation, why does the first number mentioned matter so much?
options: Anchoring: later estimates drift toward the first number, even if it's arbitrary
why: Anchoring. In experiments, even random numbers from a spinning wheel shifted people's estimates. Making a well-justified first offer often pulls the outcome your way.

title: Why quizzing yourself beats rereading

steps.p: Each time you pull a fact from memory, you strengthen the path to it. Rereading skips that effort.
Getting an answer wrong and then seeing the right one is especially memorable, even when the first attempt fails.
Quizzing again after increasing gaps — a day, a few days, a week — locks it in for the long term.

aside: This app's quizzes and review cards are built on exactly this research.

q: In one study, students estimated they'd finish their thesis in about 34 days on average. How long did they actually take?
why: About 56 days. Even their "worst case" estimates were too optimistic. Comparing with how long similar past tasks took is the best fix for the planning fallacy.

title: The two-minute rule
body: If a task takes less than two minutes, do it now. Tracking and remembering it would cost more attention than just finishing it.
challenge: Clear three tiny tasks you've been carrying around in your head in the next ten minutes.

title: Multiply by 5 in one step
body: Multiplying by 5 is the same as multiplying by 10 and halving. Halve first if the number is even.

title: Square numbers near 50
body: For 50 + a, the square is 2500 + 100a + a². So add (or subtract) 100 for each step away from 50, then add the small square.

title: Flip awkward percentages
body: x% of y always equals y% of x. When one way is hard, the other is often easy.

title: Multiply numbers equally either side of a round one
body: (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b². When two numbers are equally spaced around an easy number, square the easy number and subtract the gap squared.

q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball?
why: 5 cents. If the ball were 10 cents, the bat would be $1.10 and the total $1.20. With ball = x: x + (x + 1.00) = 1.10, so x = 0.05. Most people's fast intuition says 10 cents.

q: A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It covers the whole lake on day 48. On what day did it cover half the lake?
why: Day 47. Doubling means it was half the size just one day earlier. Exponential growth looks small for a long time, then suddenly fills everything.

q: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would 100 machines take to make 100 widgets?
why: 5 minutes. Each machine makes one widget in 5 minutes. 100 machines working in parallel make 100 widgets in the same 5 minutes.

statement: 0.999… (with nines repeating forever) is exactly equal to 1.
why: True. If x = 0.999…, then 10x = 9.999…, and subtracting gives 9x = 9, so x = 1. Another way: 1/3 = 0.333…, and three times that is 0.999… = 1.

q: How many people need to be in a room for a better than 50% chance that two share a birthday?
why: Just 23. What matters is the number of pairs: 23 people form 253 pairs. With 57 people, the chance passes 99%.

q: What is the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 100?
why: 5,050. Pair them up: 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98… gives 50 pairs of 101. The young Carl Friedrich Gauss is said to have spotted this in school.

title: There are more possible games of chess than atoms in the observable universe.
detail: Claude Shannon estimated about 10¹²⁰ possible games. The observable universe has roughly 10⁸⁰ atoms. Computers win by evaluating positions cleverly, not by exploring every game.

q: If you could fold a 0.1 mm sheet of paper in half 42 times, roughly how thick would it be?
options: About the distance to the Moon
About the width of the galaxy
why: About the distance to the Moon. 0.1 mm × 2⁴² ≈ 440,000 km, more than the Moon's average 384,000 km. Doubling is deceptively powerful.

statement: There are exactly as many even numbers as there are whole numbers.
why: True. Pair every whole number n with the even number 2n, and nothing is left over on either side. For infinite sets, "same size" means such a perfect pairing exists.

title: Spot divisibility by 3 and 9
body: A number is divisible by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3, and by 9 if they add up to a multiple of 9.

why: 9.60. 10% is 6.40, half of that (5%) is 3.20, and 6.40 + 3.20 = 9.60. Splitting percentages into 10% and 5% chunks makes them easy.
2¹⁰ = 1,024, just above 1,000. That near-coincidence is why a kilobyte is sometimes 1,000 bytes and sometimes 1,024.

q: In the classic Monty Hall game, you pick a door, the host (who knows where the car is) opens a goat door, and offers a switch. What are your odds if you switch?
why: 2/3. Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time. The host's knowing choice concentrates the remaining 2/3 onto the other closed door.
